title: How Far It Goes Before It Stops: Stopping Distance, the Speed a Sight Line Allows, and What Slope and Latency Do to Both

questions.question: The stop path waits 0.3 s. Why is that more than a software detail?
options: At 2 m/s it is 0.6 m the robot travels before the brakes are even asked
It is not: a timeout only affects how soon a message is shown
It uses memory for the whole 0.3 s
It only matters if the link is slow
questions.explanation: During the timeout the robot is still moving at full speed. Every tenth of a second of waiting is distance covered before braking starts.

questions.question: The sight line doubles from 5 m to 10 m. By how much does the allowed speed grow in the table?
options: It doubles, from 3.654 to 7.308 m/s
From 3.654 to 5.512 m/s, about 1.5 times: speed grows with the square root of the room
Not at all: speed is set by the brakes
Four times, since distance goes with the square
questions.explanation: Braking distance goes with the square of the speed, so the speed a distance allows goes with its square root. Twice the room is not twice the speed.

questions.question: What does a second of latency cost on a 3 m sight line with a deceleration of 2?
options: Nothing: latency only delays the stop
10 percent of the speed
Half the stopping distance
43 percent of the speed: 1.899 m/s against 3.347
questions.explanation: With no latency the 3 m line allows 3.347 m/s. With a second of latency, 1.899 m/s. Half a second already costs a quarter.

questions.question: On wet ground with brakes of 3 and a 17 degree downhill slope, what is the deceleration?
options: 0: friction gives 0.3 g cos(slope), gravity takes g sin(slope), and nothing is left, so the robot cannot stop by braking
3 m/s2, what the brakes give
2.94 m/s2, as on wet flat ground
1.19 m/s2, as on a 10 degree slope
questions.explanation: Wet ground at 17 degrees can give about as much grip as gravity pulls down the slope. Nothing is left for slowing down, and the formula's distance is infinite.

questions.question: Which friction and slope go into the speed limit?
options: The average over the route
The worst the machine will meet
The values the brake was tested at
The ones in the tyre's data sheet
questions.explanation: A limit set for dry flat ground is too fast everywhere else. The limit has to hold on the worst slope and surface the machine will be on.

questions.question: Why is the formula a bound to be tested and not a number to be believed?
options: The formula is only valid in simulation
It leaves out the robot's mass
It assumes constant deceleration, one friction and a known latency, and the real brake, load and surface vary: the robot must be stopped for real at the speed it gives
It is exact, so testing adds nothing
questions.explanation: It agreed with a step by step simulation to 5 mm, which shows the algebra is right. Whether the real brake and floor behave as assumed is shown by stopping the real robot.
